report.headline: REDUCE-IT succeeded with a 25% relative risk reduction (HR 0.75, p<0.001) in 8,179 high-risk patients, though the benefit is not explained by LDL-C lowering alone.
report.summary: The trial met its primary composite endpoint (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, unstable angina) with HR 0.75 (25% RRR), p<0.001, in 8,179 patients with median 4.9 years follow-up and 1,612 events. The calculator's LDL-C pathway model predicted only a 2.9% RRR (HR 0.971) based on a -6.2% LDL-C reduction, giving 8.6% power — the observed effect is far larger. Multiple biomarkers moved favorably: triglycerides -21.5%, non-HDL-C -13.6%, apoB -9.3%, hsCRP -22% (all placebo-adjusted at 12 weeks on statin background). JELIS (EPA 1.8 g/day) showed consistent benefit (HR 0.81 for major coronary events in 18,645 patients over 4.6 years). Safety profile was similar to placebo in phase 3 lipid trials (MARINE, ANCHOR). Confidence is high that the trial succeeded, but the mechanism remains uncertain (target genetics rated uncertain).
key_evidence: HR 0.75 (25% RRR), p<0.001 — source: REDUCE-IT Cardiovascular Outcomes Study of Vascepa (icosapent ethyl) Capsules Met Primary Endpoint

JELIS HR 0.81 for major coronary events in 18,645 patients over 4.6 years — source: Effects of eicosapentaenoic acid on major coronary events in hypercholesterolaemic patients (JELIS): a randomised open-label, blinded endpoint analysis.

Safety profile similar to placebo — source: Eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester (AMR101) therapy in patients with very high triglyceride levels (from the Multi-center, plAcebo-controlled, Randomized, double-blINd, 12-week study with an open-label Extension [MARINE] trial). and Efficacy and safety of eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester (AMR101) therapy in statin-treated patients with persistent high triglycerides (from the ANCHOR study).

for.text: REDUCE-IT met its primary endpoint with HR 0.75 (25% RRR), p<0.001, in 8179 patients with 1612 events over 4.9 years median follow-up.
The benefit is large and statistically robust (upper CI well below 1), consistent with JELIS (HR 0.81 for major coronary events in 18,645 patients over 4.6 years).
Multiple biomarkers moved favorably: TG -21.5%, non-HDL-C -13.6%, apoB -9.3%, hsCRP -22% (pooled phase 3), Lp-PLA2 -19% to -28%, all placebo-adjusted at 12 weeks on statin background.

against.text: The calculator's LDL-C pathway model predicts only HR 0.971 (2.9% RRR) from the -6.2% LDL-C reduction, far less than the observed 25% RRR.
Target genetics is 'uncertain' — EPA lacks a single validated molecular target with human genetic support for coronary disease.

hypotheses.would_settle: Mediation analysis of REDUCE-IT biomarker changes (TG, hsCRP, apoB, non-HDL-C, plaque imaging from EVAPORATE) to quantify contribution of each pathway to the clinical benefit.

for.text: Primary endpoint met with high statistical significance (p<0.001) and large effect size (HR 0.75), exceeding the trial's assumed 15% RRR for 90% power.
Consistent direction of benefit across components: CV death, MI, stroke, revascularization, unstable angina all favored IPE in the full publication.
Safety profile similar to placebo in phase 3 lipid trials (MARINE, ANCHOR).

against.text: Mechanism of benefit not fully explained by LDL-C lowering (only -6.2%); the calculator's LDL-C pathway accounts for <3% RRR vs observed 25%.
Mineral oil placebo may have increased LDL-C and hsCRP slightly, potentially exaggerating the treatment difference (though sensitivity analyses supported robustness).

hypotheses.would_settle: Full publication with component-level HRs, mediation analysis, and placebo lipid trajectory data.

for.text: Calculator's LDL-C pathway model yields expected HR 0.971 (causal RRR 2.9%) with only 8.6% power to detect the observed effect — the LDL-C effect alone is too small to explain the trial result.

against.text: The trial succeeded robustly (HR 0.75), proving the drug's overall effect is not too small; the calculator's model is incomplete because it only quantifies LDL-C and BP pathways, not TG, inflammation, or other pleiotropic effects.
TG reduction (-21.5%) and hsCRP reduction (-22%) are substantial; if either biomarker is causal, the expected benefit would be larger.

hypotheses.would_settle: Mendelian randomization studies clarifying causality of TG and hsCRP for ASCVD; mediation analysis in REDUCE-IT.

for.text: If the intended biomarker is triglycerides, Mendelian randomization evidence for TG as a causal factor for ASCVD is mixed — some studies support causality, others suggest it's a marker of remnant cholesterol or insulin resistance.
The calculator did not quantify a TG pathway (pathway=null), so no formal comparison of TG-mediated expected benefit vs observed is available.

against.text: Non-HDL-C and apoB (which capture remnant cholesterol) were reduced -13.6% and -9.3% respectively; these are more established causal biomarkers.
hsCRP reduction (-22%) mirrors CANTOS (canakinumab, -37% hsCRP, HR 0.85), suggesting inflammatory pathway may contribute.

hypotheses.would_settle: Genetic studies of EPA-specific pathways; mediation analysis partitioning benefit across TG, non-HDL-C, apoB, hsCRP changes.

for.text: Target genetics listed as 'uncertain' — no human genetic variant mimicking lifelong EPA supplementation shows CVD protection.

against.text: JELIS (EPA 1.8g/day) showed 19% RRR (HR 0.81) in Japanese patients; REDUCE-IT (4g/day on statins) showed 25% RRR — consistent dose-response and replication across populations.
The drug is a purified stable EPA formulation; the 'target' may be membrane incorporation, eicosanoid shift, or multiple pleiotropic effects rather than a single receptor.

hypotheses.would_settle: Genetic studies of FADS variants (affecting EPA/AA ratio) and CVD outcomes; trials of other EPA formulations.

issues.issue: Hypothesis claims about mineral oil placebo increasing LDL-C and hsCRP lack fact references (refs: []). This is a known controversy in REDUCE-IT but should be supported by a verified fact or removed.
issues.request: Add a verified fact reference for the mineral oil placebo effect on LDL-C/hsCRP, or remove the unsupported claim from the 'against' section of robust_success hypothesis.

issues.issue: Hypothesis claims about Mendelian randomization evidence for TG causality being 'mixed' and about FADS variants lack fact references (refs: []). These are substantive scientific claims that require citation.
issues.request: Add verified fact references for: (1) Mendelian randomization studies on TG and ASCVD causality, (2) FADS variant studies related to EPA/AA ratio and CVD outcomes. Search for relevant MR studies and genetic epidemiology papers.

issues.issue: The calculator uses pathway=null and falls back to LDL-C only, ignoring the intended_biomarker (triglycerides) and other favorable biomarker changes (non-HDL-C -13.6%, apoB -9.3%, hsCRP -22%). This is a known model limitation, not an input error, but the hypotheses correctly note it.
issues.request: Document that the calculator's LDL-C-only pathway model is incomplete for this mechanism. No input change needed, but ensure the 'weakest_link' and 'notes' reflect that TG, non-HDL-C, apoB, and inflammation pathways are not quantified.

issues.issue: hsCRP change input uses pooled phase 3 value (-22%) while MARINE alone showed -36% (f_0be6c87f3ab5a1). The pooled value is reasonable but the range should be noted.
issues.request: Add a note in calculator assumptions that hsCRP reduction ranged from -22% (pooled) to -36% (MARINE alone), and the pooled value was used for conservatism.
